title: Learning a distance measure from the information-estimation geometry of data
claim: A point's local gradient field reveals different geometric features of the distribution depending on noise scale, and comparing them across scales defines a distance.
layout: 3 stacked panels in perspective, left-to-right along an SNR axis, legend at top-left
description: Three slanted heatmap planes are arranged in perspective along a horizontal axis labeled gamma (SNR), which starts at 0 on the left. Each plane shows a viridis-colored Gaussian-mixture log-density, with purple at the low end and yellow at the high end. The leftmost plane is heavily blurred and shows a single merged mode. The middle plane starts to separate into two modes. The rightmost plane shows two distinct modes. Each plane has a white square marking gamma x1 and a white circle with a crimson outline marking gamma x2. Black arrows (for x1) and crimson arrows (for x2) show the gradient vectors around each point, and their opacity fades with distance from the point to suggest a Gaussian window. Black lines link the markers across planes and end in arrowheads on the right. A legend at top-left defines the symbols, and a colorbar for log p sits at bottom-left. The eye goes first to the colorful planes and the two sets of arrows.
caption: The information-estimation geometry around two points. We show a Gaussian mixture log-density and its gradient vector fields around the points $\gamma\vx_{1}$ and $\gamma\vx_{2}$ for three different SNR levels $\gamma$. The space is rescaled by $\gamma$ and the distribution collapses to a point at $\gamma=0$. When blurring the density (small $\gamma$), the two modes merge, and the gradients around $\gamma\vx_{1}$ point toward either of the modes. When the two modes are far enough apart (large $\gamma$), most gradient vectors point toward their closest mode. Thus, the local gradients around a given point can capture different geometrical features of the distribution, depending on the SNR $\gamma$. The Information-Estimation Metric (IEM, [ref]) between the two points $\vx_{1}$ and $\vx_{2}$ is the square error between the local gradient fields around them, weighted by a Gaussian window (illustrated by the opacity of the gradients' arrows) and integrated over all levels of SNR $\gamma\in[0,\Gamma]$.
abstract: We introduce the Information-Estimation Metric (IEM), a novel form of distance function derived from an underlying continuous probability density over a domain of signals. The IEM is rooted in a fundamental relationship between information theory and estimation theory, which links the log-probability of a signal with the errors of an optimal denoiser, applied to noisy observations of the signal. In particular, the IEM between a pair of signals is obtained by comparing their denoising error vectors over a range of noise amplitudes. Geometrically, this amounts to comparing the score vector fields of the blurred density around the signals over a range of blur levels. We prove that the IEM is a valid global distance metric and derive a closed-form expression for its local second-order approximation, which yields a Riemannian metric. For Gaussian-distributed signals, the IEM coincides with the Mahalanobis distance. But for more complex distributions, it adapts, both locally and globally, to the geometry of the distribution. In practice, the IEM can be computed using a learned denoiser (analogous to generative diffusion models) and solving a one-dimensional integral. To demonstrate the value of our framework, we learn an IEM on the ImageNet database. Experiments show that this IEM is competitive with or outperforms state-of-the-art supervised image quality metrics in predicting human perceptual judgments.
